decks.title: Human Health and Disease — Part 1: Common diseases in humans
goals: Explain what health means and what affects it
Describe the pathogens, symptoms and spread of common bacterial, viral, protozoan, helminth and fungal diseases
Trace the life cycle of Plasmodium
Explain how these diseases can be prevented and controlled

slides.heading: Human Health and Disease
slides.body_md: Part 1 — what health is, and the common infectious diseases, their causes and their prevention.

visual.alt: Flow from pathogen to transmission, infection and symptoms, with prevention breaking the chain

slides.narration: Health is not simply the absence of disease. It is a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being. Health is affected by our genes, by infections and by our lifestyle, including food, rest, exercise and habits. In this part we look at common infectious diseases and how to break their chains of spread.

slides.heading: What affects health
slides.body_md: Good health keeps people efficient and productive, increases longevity and reduces infant and maternal mortality. **Balanced diet, personal hygiene and regular exercise** help maintain it.

rows: Deficiencies with which a child is born
Food and water, rest and exercise, habits

visual.alt: Table of three kinds of factors that affect health with examples

slides.narration: Some threats to health come from our genes, some from infections, and many from the way we live. Infectious diseases spread from one person to another; non-infectious ones, such as cancer, do not. Awareness, vaccination, safe food and water, and clean surroundings protect whole communities.

slides.heading: Bacterial diseases: typhoid and pneumonia
slides.body_md: Disease-causing organisms are **pathogens**. Two important bacterial diseases:

rows: Small intestine first, then other organs via blood
Alveoli of the lungs (fill with fluid)
Sustained high fever (39–40 °C), weakness, stomach pain, constipation, headache, loss of appetite; intestinal perforation in severe cases
Fever, chills, cough, headache; in severe cases lips and fingernails turn grey to bluish
Droplets or aerosols from an infected person; shared glasses and utensils

visual.alt: Table comparing typhoid and pneumonia: pathogen, organ affected, symptoms, spread and notes

slides.narration: Typhoid spreads through contaminated food and water. The bacteria settle in the small intestine and spread through the blood, causing a long high fever. A famous case was a cook called Mary Mallon, a healthy carrier who spread typhoid for years. Pneumonia bacteria infect the tiny air sacs of the lungs, which fill with fluid, making breathing hard.

slides.heading: Viral and fungal diseases
slides.body_md: Viruses and fungi also cause common diseases.

rows: Infects nose and respiratory passage, not lungs; nasal congestion and discharge, sore throat, hoarseness, cough, headache; lasts 3–7 days
Droplets; contaminated objects such as pens, books, cups, doorknobs, keyboards
High fever, severe headache, pain behind the eyes, muscle and joint pain, rash; bleeding in severe cases
Dry, scaly lesions on skin, nails or scalp with intense itching; favoured by heat and moisture
Soil; sharing towels, clothes or combs

visual.alt: Table of the common cold, dengue, chikungunya and ringworm with pathogen, features and spread

slides.narration: The common cold is caused by rhinoviruses that infect the nose and throat but not the lungs, and it usually clears in a week. Dengue and chikungunya are viral fevers spread by Aedes mosquitoes, which breed in clean stagnant water around homes. Ringworm is not a worm at all but a fungal infection of the skin that thrives in warm, moist places.

slides.heading: Protozoan and helminth diseases
slides.body_md: Protozoans and parasitic worms (helminths) cause serious diseases.

rows: In the large intestine: constipation, abdominal pain and cramps, stools with excess mucus and blood clots
Contaminated food and water; houseflies carry the parasite
Internal bleeding, muscular pain, fever, anaemia, blockage of the intestinal passage
Eggs in faeces contaminate soil, water and plants; contaminated vegetables, fruits and water
Live in the lymphatic vessels of the lower limbs; chronic inflammation and swelling; genital organs may be deformed

visual.alt: Table of amoebiasis, ascariasis and filariasis with pathogen, features and spread

slides.narration: Amoebiasis is caused by a protozoan that lives in the large intestine; houseflies can carry it to food. Ascaris, a roundworm, spreads when its eggs from faeces contaminate soil and vegetables. Filarial worms live for years in lymph vessels of the legs, causing the huge swellings called elephantiasis; mosquitoes carry them from person to person.

slides.narration: An infected female Anopheles mosquito injects sporozoites with its bite. They multiply first in liver cells, then in red blood cells. When the red cells burst, they release a toxic substance called haemozoin, causing chills and high fever that recur every three to four days. Some parasites form gametocytes, which a mosquito takes up when it bites; fertilisation happens in the mosquito, and new sporozoites collect in its salivary glands.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: linking pathogen, spread and prevention
slides.body_md: A district has outbreaks of typhoid, malaria and the common cold. For each, identify the type of pathogen, the route of spread and one targeted preventive step.
bullets: Typhoid → **bacterium**; contaminated food and water → **safe drinking water and hygienic food handling**.
Malaria → **protozoan**; female Anopheles mosquito → **remove stagnant water, mosquito nets, Gambusia fish in ponds**.
Common cold → **virus**; droplets and contaminated objects → **cover coughs and sneezes, wash hands, avoid sharing cups**.
Principle — prevention works best when it blocks the **specific route** of spread.

visual.alt: Worked table linking three diseases to pathogen type, route of spread and targeted prevention

slides.narration: Ask three questions for every disease: what causes it, how does it travel, and how can we block that route? Food and water diseases need clean water and hygiene. Vector-borne diseases need mosquito control. Droplet infections need cough etiquette and clean hands. Matching the measure to the route is what makes prevention efficient.

slides.heading: Preventing and controlling infectious diseases
slides.body_md: Prevention combines **personal hygiene**, **public hygiene** and **vector control**.

rows: Clean body; safe drinking water, food, vegetables and fruits
Proper disposal of waste and excreta; periodic cleaning and disinfection of water reservoirs, pools, cesspools and tanks; standard practices in public catering
Avoid close contact with infected persons and their belongings

Avoid stagnant water around homes; clean household coolers regularly; use mosquito nets; introduce fish such as Gambusia that eat larvae; spray insecticides in ditches, drains and swamps; fit wire mesh on doors and windows

visual.alt: Table of preventive measures for infectious diseases with examples

slides.narration: Clean water, safe food and proper sanitation prevent typhoid, amoebiasis and ascariasis. For mosquito-borne diseases, the key is to stop mosquitoes breeding: do not let water stand in coolers, pots or tyres, use mosquito nets and screens, and stock ponds with Gambusia fish, which eat mosquito larvae. Vaccination and better medicines have also controlled many diseases, and smallpox has been eradicated.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: does the fish work?
slides.body_md: A village pond had about 480 mosquito larvae per sample. Two months after Gambusia fish were introduced, the count fell to 72. By what percentage did the larvae decrease?
bullets: Step 2 — Percentage decrease $= \dfrac{408}{480} \times 100 = 85$ percent.
Conclusion — biological control with larva-eating fish greatly reduces breeding of mosquitoes, without chemicals.

visual.alt: Worked table: larvae fell from 480 to 72, a 85 percent decrease

slides.narration: The fall is four hundred and eight larvae. Dividing by the starting count and multiplying by one hundred gives eighty-five percent. Fewer larvae means fewer adult mosquitoes, and so fewer cases of malaria, filariasis and dengue. Using fish to eat larvae is an example of biological control.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Health: complete physical, mental and social well-being; affected by genes, infections and lifestyle.
Bacteria: typhoid (Salmonella typhi; Widal test), pneumonia (Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae).
Viruses: common cold (rhinoviruses); dengue and chikungunya (Aedes). Fungi: ringworm (Microsporum, Trichophyton, Epidermophyton).
Protozoans: malaria (Plasmodium; female Anopheles; haemozoin), amoebiasis (Entamoeba histolytica). Helminths: ascariasis (Ascaris), filariasis (Wuchereria).
Prevention: personal and public hygiene, vector control (no stagnant water, nets, Gambusia, insecticides, wire mesh), vaccination.

visual.alt: Summary table of pathogen groups and their diseases

slides.narration: To recap: each infectious disease has a pathogen and a route of spread. Bacteria cause typhoid and pneumonia; viruses cause colds, dengue and chikungunya; protozoans cause malaria and amoebiasis; worms cause ascariasis and filariasis; fungi cause ringworm. Blocking the route, through hygiene and vector control, prevents most of them.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Learn **pathogen + symptom + spread** for each disease as a set.
For malaria, name **haemozoin**, the **female Anopheles** and the **two hosts**.
Typhoid is confirmed by the **Widal test**.
Name **Gambusia** as a biological control of mosquito larvae.
slides.narration: Exam tips. Memorise each disease as a set of pathogen, symptoms and spread. For malaria, mention haemozoin and both hosts. Remember the Widal test for typhoid. And give Gambusia as an example of biological control.

decks.title: Human Health and Disease — Part 2: Immunity and vaccines
goals: Distinguish innate and acquired immunity, and active and passive immunity
Describe the structure of an antibody and the roles of B and T lymphocytes
Explain primary and secondary immune responses and how vaccines work
Explain allergies and autoimmunity and name the lymphoid organs

slides.heading: Immunity
slides.body_md: Part 2 — how the body defends itself, and how vaccines prepare it in advance.

visual.alt: Flow from innate immunity to acquired immunity and vaccines

slides.narration: We meet pathogens every day, yet we are usually healthy. That is because of immunity, the overall ability of the body to fight disease-causing organisms. Some defences are present from birth; others are learned after meeting a pathogen and remembered for years. Vaccines use that memory.

slides.heading: Innate immunity
slides.body_md: **Innate immunity** is **non-specific** and present at **birth**. It consists of four kinds of barriers.

rows: Skin; mucus coating of the respiratory, gastrointestinal and urogenital tracts
Acid in the stomach, saliva in the mouth, tears from the eyes
Leucocytes: PMNL-neutrophils, monocytes and natural killer lymphocytes; macrophages, which engulf microbes
Interferons secreted by virus-infected cells protect non-infected cells

visual.alt: Table of the four barriers of innate immunity with examples

slides.narration: Innate immunity is our first line of defence and treats all invaders the same way. Skin and mucus keep microbes out; stomach acid, saliva and tears kill or wash them away; white blood cells such as neutrophils and macrophages swallow them; and virus-infected cells release interferons that warn their neighbours.

slides.heading: Acquired immunity
slides.body_md: **Acquired immunity** is **pathogen-specific** and has **memory**. The first encounter gives a low-intensity **primary response**; a later encounter with the same pathogen gives a highly intensified **secondary (anamnestic) response**.

rows: Produce antibodies into the blood: humoral (antibody-mediated) immunity
Help B cells produce antibodies; carry out cell-mediated immunity (CMI), including graft rejection
Remember the pathogen, giving a faster, stronger secondary response

visual.alt: Table of the roles of B-lymphocytes, T-lymphocytes and memory cells

slides.narration: Acquired immunity is like a trained army. B lymphocytes make proteins called antibodies that attack a particular pathogen. T lymphocytes help them and also attack infected cells directly. After the first fight, memory cells remain, so a second attack by the same pathogen is met quickly and strongly.

slides.heading: Primary and secondary responses
slides.body_md: After a second exposure, antibodies rise **faster** and much **higher** — in this model about 5.7 times the primary peak.

slides.narration: An antibody is shaped like the letter Y. Two long heavy chains and two short light chains are joined by disulfide bonds. The tips of the two arms are the antigen-binding sites, which fit a particular antigen like a lock and key. Different classes of antibodies, such as IgA, IgM, IgE and IgG, have different roles.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: counting chains and comparing responses
slides.body_md: (a) How many heavy and light chains are present in three antibody molecules? (b) In the model graph, the primary peak is about 19 units and the secondary peak about 108. How many times larger is the secondary peak?
bullets: (a) Each molecule is H₂L₂: heavy $= 2 \times 3 = 6$, light $= 2 \times 3 = 6$, total 12 chains.
(b) Ratio $= \dfrac{108}{19} \approx 5.7$.
Interpretation — memory cells make the secondary response several times stronger.

visual.alt: Worked table: 6 heavy and 6 light chains; secondary peak about 5.7 times the primary

slides.narration: Each antibody has two heavy and two light chains, so three antibodies have six of each, twelve chains in all. For the graph, divide the secondary peak by the primary peak; the secondary response here is several times stronger. Real values vary, but the pattern is always the same: faster and stronger the second time.

slides.heading: Active and passive immunity
slides.body_md: Immunity can be built by the body itself or given ready-made.

rows: Body makes its own antibodies after exposure to antigens (infection or vaccine)
IgA in colostrum; antibodies passing through the placenta to the foetus; anti-tetanus serum; snake antivenom

visual.alt: Table comparing active and passive immunity with examples

slides.narration: Active immunity takes time to develop, but it lasts because memory cells form. Passive immunity works at once but fades, because borrowed antibodies are eventually broken down. A baby gets passive immunity from its mother, through the placenta and through colostrum. A person bitten by a snake needs ready-made antibodies quickly, so they get antivenom.

slides.heading: Vaccination and immunisation
slides.body_md: A **vaccine** contains **antigenic proteins** of a pathogen or **inactivated or weakened** pathogens. It triggers a primary response and **memory B and T cells**, so a later infection meets a fast secondary response. **Recombinant DNA** technology allows antigens to be made in bacteria or yeast, for example the **hepatitis B vaccine** produced in yeast.

nodes.label: Vaccine: weakened or inactivated pathogen, or its antigens
Later infection: rapid, strong secondary response

visual.alt: Flow of how a vaccine leads to memory cells and a rapid response to later infection

slides.narration: A vaccine is a safe rehearsal. It shows the immune system the pathogen’s antigens without causing the disease. The body makes antibodies and memory cells. When the real pathogen arrives, the memory cells recognise it and respond strongly before it can cause illness. Mass vaccination has controlled many deadly diseases and eradicated smallpox.

slides.heading: Quick check: passive immunity
slides.body_md: Which is an example of passive immunity?
slides.narration: Quick check. Look for ready-made antibodies given from outside.

slides.heading: When immunity misfires: allergy and autoimmunity
slides.body_md: An **allergy** is an exaggerated response to certain antigens (**allergens**) such as dust mites, pollen and animal dander. **IgE** antibodies are produced; **mast cells** release chemicals such as **histamine and serotonin**. **Autoimmunity** is when the body attacks its own cells, as in **rheumatoid arthritis**.

rows: IgE made against allergens; mast cells release histamine and serotonin; sneezing, watery eyes, running nose, difficulty in breathing
Anti-histamines, adrenalin and steroids reduce symptoms

visual.alt: Table of allergy and autoimmunity with what happens and treatment or example

slides.narration: In allergies, the immune system overreacts to harmless substances like pollen or dust mites. IgE antibodies trigger mast cells to release histamine, causing sneezing and watery eyes. Modern lifestyles may lower immunity and increase sensitivity to allergens. In autoimmune diseases, the body’s defences attack its own tissues, as in rheumatoid arthritis.

slides.heading: The immune system’s organs
slides.body_md: **Lymphoid organs** are where lymphocytes originate, mature and multiply.

rows: Lymphocytes are formed and mature; antigen-sensitive cells develop
Spleen, lymph nodes, tonsils, Peyer’s patches of the small intestine, appendix
Mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue in the linings of the respiratory, digestive and urogenital tracts
About half the lymphoid tissue of the body

visual.alt: Table of primary and secondary lymphoid organs and MALT with their roles

slides.narration: Lymphocytes are born in the bone marrow; T cells mature in the thymus. They then move to secondary organs, such as the spleen, lymph nodes and tonsils, where they meet antigens and multiply. Lymph nodes trap microbes from the lymph. The thymus is large at birth and shrinks with age.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: active or passive?
slides.body_md: Classify each as active or passive immunity, and natural or artificial.
bullets: A child recovers from measles and does not get it again → **active, natural**.
A girl receives the hepatitis B vaccine → **active, artificial**.
A newborn gets antibodies through colostrum → **passive, natural**.
An injured farmer receives anti-tetanus serum → **passive, artificial**.

visual.alt: Worked table classifying four cases of immunity

slides.narration: Ask two questions. Did the body make its own antibodies? Then it is active; if they were supplied, passive. Did it happen through normal life events, or through a medical procedure? That decides natural or artificial. So recovering from measles is active and natural, while anti-tetanus serum is passive and artificial.

slides.heading: Quick check: secondary response
slides.body_md: Judge the assertion and the reason about the secondary immune response.
slides.narration: Quick check. Which cells explain the faster response?

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Innate immunity: physical, physiological, cellular and cytokine (interferon) barriers.
Acquired immunity: specific, with memory; primary and secondary (anamnestic) responses; B cells (humoral), T cells (cell-mediated).
Antibody H₂L₂; IgA, IgM, IgE, IgG.
Active (own antibodies, slow, lasting) vs passive (ready-made, quick, short). Vaccines create memory; hepatitis B vaccine from yeast.
Allergy (IgE, mast cells, histamine), autoimmunity (rheumatoid arthritis); lymphoid organs: primary (bone marrow, thymus), secondary (spleen, lymph nodes, tonsils, Peyer’s patches, appendix); MALT.

visual.alt: Summary table of types of immunity

slides.narration: To recap: innate immunity gives general protection from birth; acquired immunity is specific and remembers. Antibodies are Y-shaped proteins of four chains made by B cells. Vaccines train the immune system in advance, while passive immunity gives instant but temporary help. Sometimes the system overreacts, causing allergies, or attacks the body itself.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Draw and label an **antibody** (H₂L₂, antigen-binding sites).
Give **examples of each innate barrier**.
Contrast **active and passive** immunity with examples.
Name **IgE, mast cells, histamine** for allergy.
slides.narration: Exam tips. Practise drawing the antibody with its chains and binding sites. Learn one example for each innate barrier. Contrast active and passive immunity clearly. And for allergies, name IgE, mast cells and histamine.

decks.title: Human Health and Disease — Part 3: AIDS, cancer, and drugs and alcohol
goals: Explain how HIV is transmitted and how it causes AIDS, and how AIDS is prevented
Explain how cancer arises, its causes, detection and treatment
Describe the effects of drug and alcohol abuse, especially in adolescence
Suggest ways to prevent drug and alcohol abuse

slides.heading: AIDS, cancer, drugs and alcohol
slides.body_md: Part 3 — two major diseases and a major social health problem, with the science needed to prevent them.

visual.alt: Flow showing AIDS, cancer and drug abuse all linked to prevention through knowledge and support

slides.narration: In this part we study AIDS and cancer, two diseases that are major causes of death, and the misuse of drugs and alcohol, which harms many young people. In each case, scientific understanding helps us prevent harm and support those affected with care rather than blame.

slides.heading: HIV and its spread
slides.body_md: **AIDS** (Acquired Immuno Deficiency Syndrome), first reported in **1981**, is caused by **HIV**, a **retrovirus** with an RNA genome. There is usually a gap of **5–10 years** between infection and symptoms.

rows: Sexual contact with an infected person
Transfusion of contaminated blood or blood products
Sharing food, water or a classroom
Infected mother to child through the placenta

visual.alt: Table of ways HIV does and does not spread

slides.narration: HIV spreads only through certain body fluids: by sexual contact, infected blood, shared needles, and from an infected mother to her baby. It does not spread by everyday contact. People at higher risk include those with multiple sexual partners, drug users who share needles, and people who need repeated blood transfusions. Infected people must not be discriminated against.

slides.heading: How HIV causes AIDS
slides.body_md: HIV enters **macrophages**, where its RNA is copied into viral DNA by **reverse transcriptase**. The viral DNA joins the host DNA, so infected cells produce new viruses: the macrophage becomes an **HIV factory**. HIV then enters **helper T-lymphocytes**, multiplies, and destroys them.

nodes.label: Reverse transcriptase: viral RNA → viral DNA
Viral DNA joins host DNA; virus particles made

visual.alt: Flow of how HIV infects macrophages and helper T cells, leading to immunodeficiency and opportunistic infections

slides.narration: As helper T cells are destroyed one after another, the immune system weakens. The person suffers repeated fevers, diarrhoea and weight loss, and cannot fight infections that a healthy body controls easily, such as Mycobacterium, other viruses, fungi and parasites like Toxoplasma. These are called opportunistic infections. HIV is diagnosed by the ELISA test, and antiretroviral drugs can prolong life but cannot cure it.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: helper T-cell count
slides.body_md: A person’s helper T-cell count falls from 900 to 350 cells per microlitre of blood over several years of untreated HIV infection. By what percentage did it fall, and what does this mean?
bullets: Step 2 — Percentage fall $= \dfrac{550}{900} \times 100 \approx 61.1$ percent.
Step 3 — With fewer helper T cells, B cells make fewer antibodies and cell-mediated immunity weakens: the risk of opportunistic infections rises.

visual.alt: Worked table: helper T cells fell from 900 to 350, about 61.1 percent

slides.narration: The count dropped by five hundred and fifty cells, which is about sixty-one percent of the starting value. Helper T cells coordinate the whole acquired immune response, so losing most of them leaves the body open to infections. Antiretroviral treatment slows this fall, which is why early testing matters.

slides.heading: Preventing AIDS
slides.body_md: Since AIDS has **no cure**, **prevention** is the best option. In India, the **National AIDS Control Organisation (NACO)** and other organisations educate people.

rows: Ensure use of disposable needles and syringes
Screen blood in blood banks for HIV
Free distribution of condoms; safe sexual practices
Remove stigma so people seek testing and treatment

visual.alt: Table of measures for preventing AIDS with their purposes

slides.narration: Prevention works by blocking each route: safe needles, screened blood, condoms and safe practices, and control of drug abuse. Equally important is ending stigma. If people fear being shunned, they avoid testing. Treating HIV-positive people with dignity helps everyone, because it encourages early testing and treatment.

slides.heading: Quick check: HIV
slides.body_md: Which cells does HIV mainly destroy, leading to immunodeficiency?
slides.narration: Quick check. Which T cells coordinate the immune response?

slides.heading: Cancer: cells out of control
slides.body_md: Normal cells show **contact inhibition**: contact with other cells stops their division. **Cancer cells lose this property**, divide without control and form **tumours**.

rows: Stays confined to its original location
Grows rapidly and invades surrounding tissues
Spreads to distant sites through blood: metastasis

visual.alt: Table comparing benign and malignant tumours

slides.narration: Normally, our cells divide only as needed and stop when they touch neighbours. Cancer cells ignore these signals. Benign tumours stay in one place. Malignant tumours are made of neoplastic cells that invade nearby tissues, starve normal cells of nutrients, and can travel through the blood to form new tumours far away. This spread, called metastasis, makes cancer so dangerous.

slides.heading: Causes, detection and treatment of cancer
slides.body_md: **Carcinogens** transform normal cells into cancer cells. Genes called **cellular oncogenes (proto-oncogenes)** can become activated and cause cancer.

rows: Ionising radiations (X-rays, gamma rays) and non-ionising radiation (UV)
Tobacco smoke (main cause of lung cancer) and other chemicals
Biopsy and histopathology; blood and bone-marrow tests for leukaemia; X-rays, CT and MRI; antibodies against cancer-specific antigens; molecular tests for inherited susceptibility
Surgery, radiation therapy, chemotherapy (side effects such as hair loss, anaemia), immunotherapy with biological response modifiers such as α-interferon

visual.alt: Table of the causes, detection and treatment of cancer

slides.narration: Cancer can be triggered by radiation, by chemicals such as those in tobacco smoke, and by some viruses. Early detection saves lives: doctors use biopsies, scans like CT and MRI, blood tests and molecular tests. Treatment usually combines surgery, radiation and drugs, and some therapies boost the patient’s own immune system to destroy the tumour.

slides.heading: Quick check: metastasis
slides.body_md: Judge the assertion and the reason about tumours.
slides.narration: Quick check. What lets cancer cells form tumours far from the original one?

slides.heading: Commonly abused drugs
slides.body_md: Drugs are often obtained from plants or fungi. Their misuse harms the body and mind.

rows: Morphine from the latex of the poppy, Papaver somniferum
Bind opioid receptors in the brain and gut; heroin is a depressant that slows body functions
Interferes with dopamine transport; stimulation and false euphoria; excessive use causes hallucinations

visual.alt: Table of commonly abused drugs with their sources and effects

slides.narration: Many drugs come from plants. Heroin is made from morphine, which comes from the poppy. Marijuana and similar drugs come from Cannabis. Cocaine comes from the coca plant and interferes with a brain chemical called dopamine. Some medicines, such as barbiturates, amphetamines and benzodiazepines, are also misused. All of them change how the brain works and can be very harmful.

slides.heading: Tobacco and alcohol
slides.body_md: **Tobacco** contains the alkaloid **nicotine**, which stimulates the adrenal gland to release **adrenaline and nor-adrenaline**, raising blood pressure and heart rate. **Alcohol** damages the nervous system and liver.

rows: Cancers of the lung, urinary bladder and throat; bronchitis, emphysema, coronary heart disease, gastric ulcer; carbon monoxide reduces oxygen carried by haemoglobin
Damage to the nervous system and liver (cirrhosis); harm to the foetus during pregnancy

visual.alt: Table of harms of smoking, chewing tobacco and chronic alcohol use

slides.narration: Tobacco smoke carries nicotine and carbon monoxide. Nicotine raises blood pressure and heart rate, and carbon monoxide reduces the oxygen the blood can carry. Smoking causes cancers and lung and heart diseases. Alcohol, taken regularly, damages the brain and liver. Many habits that start in the teenage years become hard to break later.

slides.heading: Adolescence, addiction and dependence
slides.body_md: **Adolescence** (about **12–18 years**) is a vulnerable period. Curiosity, the need for adventure and excitement, experimentation, stress, peer pressure and media influence can lead to first use. Repeated use can cause **addiction** (psychological attachment) and **dependence**, with a **withdrawal syndrome** (anxiety, shakiness, nausea, sweating) when use stops.

rows: Drop in academic performance; absence from school
Loss of interest in hobbies and hygiene
Overdose can cause coma and death (respiratory or heart failure, brain haemorrhage)
Withdrawal from friends and family; mood changes
Sharing needles spreads HIV and hepatitis B
Anabolic steroids misused in sport cause hormonal and organ damage

visual.alt: Table of warning signs of drug misuse and its harms

slides.narration: Adolescents may try drugs or alcohol out of curiosity, to fit in with friends, or to escape stress. The brain soon starts to depend on them, and stopping causes unpleasant withdrawal symptoms. Families and teachers can watch for warning signs, such as falling grades and withdrawal from friends, and offer support early.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: reading a survey
slides.body_md: In a survey of 60 students, 18 said they had tried smoking because friends pressured them. What percentage is this, and what does it suggest for prevention?
bullets: Step 1 — Percentage $= \dfrac{18}{60} \times 100 = 30$ percent.
Step 2 — Nearly one in three cited peer pressure.
Conclusion — programmes should build skills to say no, involve peers and parents, and offer counselling, not just give information.

rows: Tried smoking due to peer pressure

visual.alt: Worked table: 18 of 60 students, 30 percent

slides.narration: Eighteen out of sixty is thirty percent. If peer pressure is such a common reason, prevention should focus on helping young people resist it: confidence, support from friends and family, and easy access to counselling. Information alone is not enough.

slides.heading: Prevention and control of drug and alcohol abuse
slides.body_md: Prevention is better than cure, and it starts at home and school.

rows: Respect each child’s choices and pace; do not push them beyond their abilities
Teach how to face problems, stress and failure; channel energy into sports, music, reading and other activities
Seek help from parents and peers
Trusted adults and friends can guide and support
Parents and teachers notice early and act
Psychologists, psychiatrists, de-addiction and rehabilitation programmes help recovery

visual.alt: Table of measures to prevent and control drug and alcohol abuse

slides.narration: Many problems can be prevented when young people feel supported. Parents and teachers should avoid putting undue pressure on children, encourage healthy activities, and talk openly. Anyone struggling with drugs or alcohol can recover with professional help from counsellors, doctors and de-addiction programmes. Asking for help is a sign of strength.

slides.heading: Quick check: nicotine
slides.body_md: How does nicotine raise blood pressure and heart rate?
slides.narration: Quick check. Which gland does nicotine stimulate?

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: AIDS: HIV (retrovirus); spread by sexual contact, blood, needles, mother to child; enters macrophages (reverse transcriptase), destroys helper T cells; opportunistic infections; ELISA; antiretroviral drugs; prevention via NACO measures and ending stigma.

Cancer: loss of contact inhibition; benign vs malignant (metastasis); carcinogens (radiation, chemicals, oncogenic viruses), proto-oncogenes; detection (biopsy, CT, MRI, molecular tests); treatment (surgery, radiation, chemotherapy, immunotherapy with α-interferon).
Drugs: opioids (heroin from morphine, poppy), cannabinoids, cocaine; tobacco (nicotine, CO), alcohol (liver cirrhosis).
Adolescence (12–18 years): curiosity, peer pressure; addiction, dependence, withdrawal; prevention through support, education, counselling, professional help.

visual.alt: Summary table of key words for AIDS, cancer and drug abuse

slides.narration: To recap: HIV destroys helper T cells, causing AIDS; prevention and kindness are our best tools. Cancer arises when cells lose control of division; early detection and combined treatment save lives. Drugs, tobacco and alcohol harm the body and mind, especially in adolescence, and support from family, friends and professionals is the best prevention.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Write the **sequence of HIV infection** in order: macrophage → reverse transcriptase → HIV factory → helper T cells.
Contrast **benign and malignant** tumours; define **metastasis**.
Give **three types of carcinogens** with examples.
For drug-abuse questions, include **causes, effects and prevention**.
slides.narration: Exam tips. Learn the HIV sequence in order. Contrast benign and malignant tumours and define metastasis. Give examples for physical, chemical and biological carcinogens. And in drug-abuse answers, cover causes, effects and prevention.

sections.heading: 1. Health and common diseases
sections.body_md:
**Health** is a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being. It is affected by **genetic disorders**, **infections** and **lifestyle** (food and water, rest and exercise, habits). Disease-causing organisms are **pathogens**.

| Disease | Pathogen | Main symptoms | Spread |
|---|---|---|---|
| Typhoid | *Salmonella typhi* (bacterium) | Sustained high fever (39–40 °C), weakness, stomach pain, constipation, headache, loss of appetite; intestinal perforation in severe cases; **Widal test** | Contaminated food and water |
| Pneumonia | *Streptococcus pneumoniae*, *Haemophilus influenzae* | Alveoli fill with fluid; fever, chills, cough, headache; lips and nails grey to bluish in severe cases | Droplets, aerosols, shared glasses and utensils |
| Common cold | Rhinoviruses | Nose and respiratory passage (not lungs); congestion, discharge, sore throat, hoarseness, cough, headache; 3–7 days | Droplets; contaminated objects |
| Dengue | Dengue virus | High fever, severe headache, pain behind the eyes, muscle and joint pain, rash; bleeding when severe | *Aedes* mosquitoes |
| Chikungunya | Chikungunya virus | Fever with severe joint pain | *Aedes* mosquitoes |
| Malaria | *Plasmodium* (*P. vivax*, *P. malariae*, *P. falciparum*) | Haemozoin from burst RBCs: chill and high fever every 3–4 days; *P. falciparum* malignant | Female *Anopheles* mosquito |
| Amoebiasis | *Entamoeba histolytica* | Constipation, abdominal pain, cramps, stools with mucus and blood clots | Contaminated food and water; houseflies as carriers |
| Ascariasis | *Ascaris* (roundworm) | Internal bleeding, muscular pain, fever, anaemia, intestinal blockage | Eggs from faeces contaminate soil, water, vegetables |
| Filariasis (elephantiasis) | *Wuchereria bancrofti*, *W. malayi* | Chronic inflammation of lymphatic vessels of lower limbs; genital deformity | Bite of female mosquito vectors |
| Ringworm | *Microsporum*, *Trichophyton*, *Epidermophyton* (fungi) | Dry scaly lesions on skin, nails, scalp; intense itching; heat and moisture help | Soil; shared towels, clothes, combs |

sections.heading: 2. Malaria life cycle; prevention and control
sections.body_md:
**Plasmodium** needs two hosts. Female *Anopheles* injects **sporozoites** → multiply in **liver cells** → attack **RBCs**, multiply, burst them (haemozoin: chill and fever every 3–4 days) → **gametocytes** form in RBCs → taken up by a female *Anopheles* → **fertilisation and development in the mosquito's stomach wall** → sporozoites stored in the **salivary glands** → injected at the next bite.

**Prevention and control:**
- **Personal hygiene:** clean body; safe drinking water, food, vegetables and fruits.
- **Public hygiene:** proper disposal of waste and excreta; periodic cleaning and disinfection of water reservoirs, pools, cesspools and tanks; standard practices in public catering.
- **Air-borne diseases:** avoid close contact with infected persons and their belongings.
- **Vector-borne diseases** (malaria, filariasis, dengue, chikungunya): avoid stagnant water near homes; clean household coolers regularly; use mosquito nets; introduce **Gambusia** fish that feed on mosquito larvae; spray insecticides in ditches, drainage areas and swamps; fit wire mesh on doors and windows.
- **Vaccination** and modern medicines have controlled many diseases; smallpox has been eradicated.

A fish that eats mosquito larvae; used in biological control.

sections.heading: 3. Immunity
sections.body_md:
**Innate immunity** (non-specific, present at birth): **physical** barriers (skin, mucus of respiratory, gastrointestinal and urogenital tracts); **physiological** (stomach acid, saliva, tears); **cellular** (PMNL-neutrophils, monocytes, natural killer lymphocytes, macrophages); **cytokine** (interferons from virus-infected cells).

**Acquired immunity** (pathogen-specific, with **memory**): primary response of low intensity; **secondary (anamnestic)** response highly intensified. **B-lymphocytes** produce **antibodies** (humoral immunity); **T-lymphocytes** help B cells and mediate **cell-mediated immunity** (CMI), which is responsible for **graft rejection** (hence tissue and blood-group matching and immunosuppressants).

**Antibody:** four polypeptide chains, two heavy and two light (**H₂L₂**); IgA, IgM, IgE, IgG.

**Active immunity:** the host makes antibodies after exposure to antigens (infection or vaccine); slow, long-lasting. **Passive immunity:** ready-made antibodies given — colostrum (IgA), antibodies through the placenta, anti-tetanus serum, snake antivenom; quick, short-lived.

**Vaccination:** antigenic proteins or inactivated/weakened pathogens produce memory B and T cells; a later exposure gives a rapid, massive response. **Recombinant DNA** technology allows antigens to be produced in bacteria or yeast (hepatitis B vaccine from yeast).

**Allergy:** exaggerated response to allergens (dust mites, pollen, animal dander); **IgE**; mast cells release **histamine and serotonin**; treated with anti-histamines, adrenalin, steroids. **Autoimmunity:** attack on self cells, e.g. **rheumatoid arthritis**.

**Lymphoid organs:** primary — **bone marrow, thymus**; secondary — **spleen, lymph nodes, tonsils, Peyer's patches, appendix**; **MALT** forms about half the lymphoid tissue.

sections.heading: 4. AIDS
sections.body_md:
**AIDS** (Acquired Immuno Deficiency Syndrome), first reported in **1981**, is caused by **HIV**, a **retrovirus** with an RNA genome. **Transmission:** sexual contact with an infected person; transfusion of contaminated blood or blood products; sharing infected needles; infected mother to child through the placenta. Not by casual contact. Time lag of **5–10 years** from infection to symptoms.

**How it acts:** HIV enters **macrophages**; RNA → viral DNA by **reverse transcriptase**; viral DNA incorporated into host DNA; infected cells make virus particles (macrophage as an **HIV factory**); HIV enters **helper T-lymphocytes**, replicates and destroys them; their number falls; immunodeficiency leads to **opportunistic infections** (Mycobacterium, viruses, fungi, *Toxoplasma*).

**Diagnosis:** **ELISA**. **Treatment:** antiretroviral drugs (partly effective; prolong life). **Prevention:** NACO and other organisations; disposable needles and syringes; screening of blood; condoms and safe practices; control of drug abuse; regular check-ups for susceptible groups; awareness and acceptance rather than stigma.

key_terms.definition_md: A virus with an RNA genome that is copied into DNA by reverse transcriptase.
Infection by organisms that a healthy immune system would normally control.

visual.alt: Flow of HIV infection to AIDS

sections.heading: 5. Cancer
sections.body_md:
Normal cells show **contact inhibition**; cancer cells lose it and divide uncontrollably, forming **tumours**. **Benign** tumours stay confined and cause little damage. **Malignant** tumours grow rapidly, invade surrounding tissues and spread to distant sites through blood (**metastasis**).

**Causes (carcinogens):** physical — ionising radiations (X-rays, gamma rays) and non-ionising UV; chemical — tobacco smoke (major cause of lung cancer); biological — oncogenic viruses with viral oncogenes. **Cellular oncogenes (c-onc, proto-oncogenes)** in normal cells can be activated and cause cancer.

**Detection:** biopsy and histopathology; blood and bone marrow tests (leukaemia); radiography, CT (computed tomography) and MRI (magnetic resonance imaging); antibodies against cancer-specific antigens; molecular techniques to detect genes for inherited susceptibility.

**Treatment:** surgery, radiation therapy, chemotherapy (side effects such as hair loss and anaemia), immunotherapy with **biological response modifiers** such as **α-interferon**; usually a combination.

key_terms.definition_md: Property of normal cells by which contact with other cells stops their division.
Spread of cancer cells through the blood to form new tumours at distant sites.

sections.heading: 6. Drugs and alcohol abuse
sections.body_md:
**Commonly abused drugs:**
- **Opioids** bind opioid receptors in the CNS and gut. **Heroin** (smack, diacetylmorphine) is made by acetylation of **morphine** from the latex of the poppy (*Papaver somniferum*); a depressant that slows body functions.
- **Cannabinoids** (marijuana, hashish, charas, ganja) from *Cannabis sativa*; affect the cardiovascular system.
- **Cocaine** from *Erythroxylum coca*; interferes with **dopamine** transport; stimulation and euphoria; excessive doses cause hallucinations. Other hallucinogens: *Atropa belladonna*, *Datura*. Medicines such as barbiturates, amphetamines and benzodiazepines are also misused.

**Tobacco:** **nicotine** stimulates the adrenal gland to release **adrenaline and nor-adrenaline**, raising blood pressure and heart rate. Smoking causes cancers of lung, urinary bladder and throat, bronchitis, emphysema, coronary heart disease and gastric ulcer; **CO** reduces oxygen bound to haemoglobin. Chewing tobacco causes oral cancer.

**Adolescence (12–18 years):** curiosity, adventure, experimentation, stress, peer pressure, media. Repeated use → **addiction** and **dependence**, with a **withdrawal syndrome** (anxiety, shakiness, nausea, sweating). **Effects:** reckless behaviour, vandalism, violence; overdose may cause coma and death; shared needles spread HIV and hepatitis B; chronic alcohol damages the nervous system and liver (cirrhosis) and harms the foetus. Misuse of **anabolic steroids** in sport causes hormonal and organ damage.

**Prevention:** avoid undue peer pressure; education and counselling; help from parents and peers; looking for danger signs; professional and medical help (de-addiction and rehabilitation).

key_terms.definition_md: Psychological attachment to the effects of a drug or alcohol.
The body’s need for a drug, shown by withdrawal symptoms when it is stopped.
Unpleasant symptoms (anxiety, shakiness, nausea, sweating) when regular drug use stops.

**Common mistakes**
- Saying ringworm is caused by a worm (it is a fungal infection).
- Naming the male mosquito, or Culex, as the malaria vector (it is the female Anopheles).
- Saying HIV destroys B cells (it destroys helper T cells, after infecting macrophages).
- Mixing up active and passive immunity.
- Describing benign tumours as spreading (only malignant tumours metastasise).
- Saying nicotine lowers blood pressure.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1-mark items: pathogen, vector, test, term or example.
- 2–3-mark answers: cause + symptom + prevention; mechanism steps in order; comparison points.
- 5-mark answers: life cycle of Plasmodium, HIV and AIDS, or cancer (causes, detection, treatment), with a diagram or flow chart.
- Case-based items: outbreak data, antibody graphs or survey numbers, with a 2-mark part with an internal choice.

questions.stem_md: Describe the life cycle of Plasmodium in its two hosts with the help of a labelled flow diagram. Suggest two measures to control malaria based on this life cycle.

answer.model_answer_md:
**In humans.** When an infected female Anopheles mosquito bites, it injects sporozoites, the infective stage. They multiply in the liver cells, then attack red blood cells, where they multiply further and cause the RBCs to burst. The rupture releases haemozoin, which causes chill and high fever recurring every three to four days. Some parasites develop into gametocytes in the RBCs.

**In the mosquito.** When a female Anopheles bites an infected person, it takes up gametocytes with the blood. Fertilisation and development take place in the mosquito’s stomach, and the sporozoites formed move to its salivary glands, ready to be injected at the next bite.

**Diagram:** sporozoites → liver cells → RBCs (haemozoin, fever) → gametocytes → mosquito stomach (fertilisation) → salivary glands → sporozoites.

**Control.** Break the cycle at the mosquito: remove stagnant water, introduce Gambusia fish to eat larvae, spray insecticides in breeding areas, and use mosquito nets and wire mesh to prevent bites; treat patients early so that fewer gametocytes reach mosquitoes.

questions.solution_md: Two hosts, stages in order, control based on the cycle.

questions.stem_md: Explain how normal cells become cancerous, and describe the methods used to detect and treat cancer.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Transformation.** Normal cells show contact inhibition: contact with neighbouring cells stops their division. Cancer cells lose this property and divide uncontrollably, forming tumours. answer.model_answer_md:
**How HIV spreads.** HIV is transmitted by sexual contact with an infected person, transfusion of contaminated blood or blood products, sharing infected needles, and from an infected mother to her child. **Evaluation.** Excluding the student would not protect anyone, because ordinary school activities carry no risk of transmission. It would harm the student’s education and health, spread fear and stigma, and discourage others from getting tested, which makes the epidemic harder to control.

**What the school should do.** Keep the student’s status confidential; educate students and staff about the real routes of transmission; follow standard first-aid hygiene, such as using gloves when handling blood, which protects everyone regardless of status; and support awareness programmes like those of NACO.

**Conclusion.** The proposal is not justified; inclusion with education is both safe and fair.

questions.stem_md: Plan a programme for a secondary school to prevent drug and alcohol abuse among adolescents. Justify each part of your plan using what you know about why adolescents start using drugs and how dependence develops.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Why adolescents start.** Adolescence (about 12–18 years) is a time of curiosity, a wish for adventure and excitement, experimentation, stress from studies or family, peer pressure and media influence. 1. Life-skills sessions on handling stress, failure and peer pressure, including practising refusal — because peer pressure and stress are common triggers.

3. Sports, arts, music and clubs — because they channel energy and offer healthy excitement.

5. A confidential counsellor and links to doctors and de-addiction centres — because dependence needs professional help.
